body_markdown:
Upon its debut in late 1953, the General Motors PD-4501 motor coach—perhaps better known as the Greyhound Scenicruiser—turned heads with its unique split-level roofline, well-appointed interior, and expansive views of the surrounding world. Equally distinctive, but far less visible to most, was the Scenicruiser’s powertrain, which used not one, but two diesel engines.


Look, Ma—two diesels!


GM


By the time Scenicruisers hit the road en masse *,* packing two powerplants into a motorcoach wasn’t entirely a new idea for Greyhound Lines. Nor, for that matter, was the idea of having GM Truck & Coach build a unique design exclusively for its fleet. After all, the carrier had inked a deal with Yellow Truck & Coach for that purpose in 1929, four years after GM bought a sizable chunk of John Hertz’s manufacturing consortium in order to enter the bus business. Coaches like the Yellow 719/ 743 and the later “Silversides” models (both styled in large part by[industrial design magnate Raymond Loewy](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/4-fireside-worthy-books-about-the-men-and-women-who-designed-our-world/) ) infused Greyhound’s fleet with pizazz and passenger amenities that often couldn’t be found elsewhere, even in Yellow/GM’s other coach models.


Early prototype for the Yellow/Greyhound Model 719, which would establish the mold for American motorcoaches for decades to come.


GM


At the close of World War II, Greyhound brass, led by then-president Orville Caesar, began ideating an all-new bus that could transport 50 passengers in air-sprung, air-conditioned comfort. From square one, Greyhound engineers seemed keen on a twin-engine concept, utilizing two smaller-displacement engines paired together instead of one larger powerplant.[Greyhound’s original patent for the dual-drive system](https://patents.google.com/patent/US2689013A/en?oq=US2%2c689%2c013%2c) touted a number of theoretical advantages, chief among them the ability to shut off the additional engine on flat stretches of interstate, potentially reducing fuel consumption.


1948 GX-1 “Highway Traveler.”


Bettmann Archive/Getty Images


The completed 1948 GX-1 “Highway Traveler” prototype, developed and built in-house by Greyhound, put that theory to the test. The hulking 35-foot double-decker bus was powered by a pair of air-cooled Franklin O-335 horizontally opposed six-cylinder engines (essentially the very engine later adapted for use in the[production-spec 1948 Tucker automobile](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/tucker-the-man-the-machine-the-dream/) ).


Overhead view of GX-1’s pair of Franklin flat-sixes.


USTPO


Tucker-ized version of the O-335.


Evan McCausland


Slightly saner heads prevailed when work began on the GX-1’s successor. At that point, Greyhound was convinced it needed a bus no less than 40 feet in length in order to schlep more than 35 passengers and their belongings—a challenge in itself, as most laws restricted intercity buses to 35 feet. The next prototype, the 40-foot GX-2 “Scenicruiser” of 1949, was developed with considerable input and support from General Motors’ styling and engineering staff. The latter even shipped an existing bus to Greyhound’s engineering teams to serve as the basis for the new prototype.


[Embed from Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/82139329)


Expansive view ahead through GX-2’s vista dome.


GM


Electro-Motive’s *Train of Tomorrow* , complete with Vista Domes


Gamma-Keystone/Getty Images


The GX-2 ditched the double-decker configuration of its predecessor in favor of a staggered “deck-and-a-half” design, which treated those seated up above to an expansive forward-facing “vista dome.” (It was likely inspired in part by GM’s *Train of Tomorrow* , built a few years prior.) The GX-2 also ditched the dueling Franklins for a single engine: a 6.9-liter, two-stroke GM[Detroit Diesel](https://www.hagerty.com/media/archived/behemoth-two-stroke-detroit-diesel-is-king/) 6-71 inline-six, paired with a four-speed manual transmission. While this engine had already proven reliable in several different industries, it wound up being woefully underpowered for GX-2’s added length and heft.


Between 1952 and 1953, GM and Greyhound worked to refine and iterate the Scenicruiser concept, ultimately creating a model intended for production known as the PD-4501. Because it was developed alongside the 35-foot PD-4104 coach, the two share a number of details, including air suspension and many exterior styling cues.


These images show EXP-331, the prototype PD-4501.


GM


GM


Passengers on a Greyhound dual-level Scenicruiser bus ride in comfort with reclining seats and complete washroom facilities, 1957.


Getty Images


[Embed from Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/78970692)


They couldn’t, however, share engines. While the 4104 was lithe enough to run a 210-horsepower version of the 6-71, the engine was still deemed insufficient for the larger 4501. GM didn’t have an ideal alternative at the time, since the Series 71 engine range topped out at the 6-71. The next step up in its diesel portfolio, the gargantuan 10.8-liter Detroit Diesel 6-110, would have served up over 300 hp, but it also would have been egregiously heavy and a packaging nightmare.


GM


GM


GM


GM


The solution: Go back to Greyhound’s drawing board and implement a variation of the twin-engine arrangement. Engineers cribbed a pair of marine-block 4-71 diesels (with blocks canted at 70 degrees in order to fit below the deck of a boat), mounted them in a V-shape on a removable subframe, then bolted their crankshaft outputs to a fluid coupling assembly. The single output was then connected to a three-speed manual transmission and an electrically controlled two-speed auxiliary “splitter” transmission.


Although there remains some debate as to whether or not a Scenicruiser could actually operate on a single engine as intended in the GX-1, most accounts hold the 4501 could do so, albeit only as an emergency means to limp a hobbled coach to the nearest station or service center. In normal use, the coach was designed to fire up and run both engines, thus abandoning Greyhound’s original fuel-saving strategy.


GM


Despite the stalwart nature of the Series 71 engines and the success GM enjoyed with fluid couplings elsewhere across its sprawling organization (looking at you, Hydra-Matic and Allison), the Scenicruiser’s unique powertrain quickly became its Achilles’ heel. A *Motor Coach Age* retrospective reported Greyhound was hounding GM about mechanical difficulties, mostly tied to the fluid coupling and twin-engine arrangement, while GM was only halfway through manufacturing the 1001-unit production run. These issues likely also scared customers away from the proposed PD-4901, essentially a single-story clone of the Scenicruiser intended for non-Greyhound entities.


Only one PD-4901 was built, which miraculously still exists today.


GM


Patience on Greyhound’s end was likely thinner than ever, thanks to a management shake-up resulting in a new regime that seemed less open to mechanical experimentation than Caesar’s team had been. The two companies notoriously quarreled publicly—even legally, briefly—but found some semblance of a détente, as Greyhound placed a sizable order of PD-4104s between 1957 and 1958, and continued ordering small quantities of 35-foot GM coaches in following years.


That said, the Scenicruiser fall-out (along with an ongoing antitrust suit that focused largely upon GM’s exclusivity arrangement with Greyhound) led the carrier to invest further in Motor Coach Industries, a rival bus manufacturer based in Winnipeg, Alberta, Canada. It effectively became Greyhound’s in-house bus manufacturer. Future Greyhound orders would increasingly shift toward MCI products as the manufacturer scaled up its abilities and refined its designs to Greyhound’s tastes.


By late 1956 and early 1957, Greyhound began the process of exchanging the Scenicruiser’s double-diesel powertrain for a simpler, single-engine affair. Greyhound tested a number of options, including some Mack powerplants, and popular legend suggests Greyhound went so far as to ship a PD-4501 to Germany for Mercedes-Benz powertrain engineers to tinker with, although there seems to be little public corroborating evidence of this trip on record.


At long last, the 8V-71.


GM


Concurrently, Detroit Diesel *finally* managed to expand the Series 71 engine family with V-block engines in 1957, including the eight-cylinder, 9.3-liter 8V-71. While specifications varied between applications, most 8V-71s not only fit within the confines of the Scenicruiser’s engine bay but also produced roughly the same power as the pair of 4-71s yielded on a good day.


The 8V-71 as retrofitted to Scenicruiser #001.


Mecum


Some Scenicruiser histories suggest GM had no interest in helping Greyhound with an engine swap, but records do indicate that GM field service engineers were involved in validating the 8V-71 package, which also ditched the three-speed transmission and splitter box for a standard four-speed manual transmission. Beginning in 1961, Greyhound contracted the actual conversion work to[Marmon-Herrington in Indiana,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/rare-1948-ford-marmon-herrington-eye-candy/) while tasking its own repair facilities with overhauling the remainder of the coach structure.


Mecum


Mecum


Scenicruiser #001 was restored by Greyhound in the late 1970s, utilizing many new-old-stock parts that were then still available.


Every single Scenicruiser—even the first production unit, which is arguably one of the most original examples left today,[and will soon be up for grabs at Mecum’s Las Vegas auction](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1173059/1954-gmc-pd4501-scenicruiser-passenger-bus/) —was stripped of its original powertrain and given an 8V-71.


Interestingly, some rarely viewed internal GM documents suggest the engine swap may not have been the first method for resolution for either Greyhound or GM.


GM


GM


GM PD-4902 Prototype


Upon the debut of the 8V-71, GM started designing new buses around that engine, including this previously unseen 40-foot PD-4902 prototype. Contrary to some accounts that suggest the 4902 never escaped the drawing board, these photos show it escaped both the draft room and the engineering garage. Likewise, an internal GM memo from March 1968 reflecting on the troubled state of the company’s coach operations recalls that the PD-4902 was engineered and tooled to the point where an operating, production-intent sample had been shown and pitched to both Greyhound and its largest rival, Continental Trailways, in late 1958.


GM PD-4902 Prototype


GM


Trailways was certainly an eager prospect. Caught flat-footed by the launch of the Scenicruiser and unable to find a suitable rival of its own domestically, it developed the Golden Eagle, its own 40-foot coach design, in partnership with German bus builder Kässbohrer. Unfortunately, Trailways found its reliability unsatisfactory. Stocking and servicing European components across America proved challenging, to say the least.


Trailways was allegedly convinced enough by the 4902 prototype to commit to an order for 200 units. Greyhound’s management, however, told GM reps it no longer saw the need for 40-foot coaches and passed on the idea. GM subsequently canceled the project in mid-1959, which infuriated Trailways. It increased its investment in manufacturing Eagle coaches in order to further shift away from buying GM products.


If Trailways’ pullback didn’t already sting, that same 1968 memo claims Greyhound had an about-face the very next year. “When it became evident to Greyhound that Trailways was dedicated to pursuing the Eagle further,” it reads, “\[Greyhound\] realized its decision for no additional 40-foot coaches could not stand. Since GM had scrapped the 40-foot intercity program, the only immediate alternative was a complete repowering and rehabilitation program for the Scenicruisers.”


GM wouldn’t launch another 40-foot intercity coach until 1968, with the PD-4903 shown here.


GM


This 35-foot 1967 PD-4107 was one of the last GM intercity coaches purchased new by Greyhound.


GM


GM would finally offer a 40-foot intercity coach once again a full decade later, but the damage was done. With Trailways and Greyhound both effectively building their own coaches, the country’s largest intercity bus operators bought fewer and fewer coaches from GM, leaving a former juggernaut of the industry to chase after crumbs in an already low-volume market. Between 1975 and 1979, GM sold no more than 230 intercity coaches annually, ultimately leading it to abandon the segment altogether in 1980.


Any cylinder count you’d like, so long as it’s no more than six.


GM
